summary:
Homosexuality has been legal in Monaco since the 18th century. Hate-motivated conduct on the basis of sexual orientation is criminalised in several statutes: Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence; Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years; and Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 inserted sexual orientation into Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts, attacks on a partner or co-resident, and unprovoked attacks on a person or group. A Monegasque court applied this framework in July 2010, sentencing a man to five days' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine for homophobic rhetoric against a gay man.

There is no general statutory ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Outright International states plainly that such discrimination is not prohibited, while Queer In The World describes prohibitions as existing only in certain contexts; reported discrimination is characterised as rare. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill would have required annual anti-discrimination teaching in primary and secondary schools covering sexual orientation, but the Council of Government did not approve it and the replacement adopted on 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Trans visitors should note that Monaco does not permit transgender people to alter their legal gender, a limitation recorded by ILGA-Europe, which ranked the principality 45th of 49 European countries in 2019. The same monitor's framework does not bind Monaco, which is not a member of the European Union, although it maintains close cultural and economic ties with France.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised and same-sex couples have no right to adopt. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, a cohabitation agreement introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, approved unanimously by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and lodged with a public registry, and cohabiting couples are taxed as siblings rather than as spouses. The arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no access to equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave.

The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report recorded no significant changes and no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses; the significant issues it identified were libel and lèse-majesté provisions, described as not enforced. No anti-trans incidents are reported in the sources, and no bathroom or facility restrictions appear on record. Entry is normally made across the short land frontier with France under the common border-free travel zone; the principality covers roughly 200 hectares and is heavily policed.

Visibility remains very limited. No Pride event is held anywhere in Monaco, there are no official gay bars, clubs or events, and an estimated 10 people are openly out. Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relations.
tangentialFactors:
Monaco sits near the bottom of European LGBT-rights assessments. ILGA-Europe placed it 45th of 49 European countries in 2019, and a Council of Europe rapporteur, Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo, summarised the record as "C'est le triste bilan de Monaco". The comparison with France is structural as well as geographic: Monaco is not in the European Union, so EU anti-discrimination and equality directives do not apply there, while France handles Monaco's defence through a National Guard arrangement and permits openly LGBT people to serve.

Nearby French cities supply the regional contrast. Visitors are directed to Marseille, Nice and Lyon, or to Italy, for Pride and for established gay venues, since none operate inside the principality. The state is marketed as a luxury and relaxation destination with LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation but no discernible local scene.

Family-law gaps have knock-on effects beyond couples: the absence of joint adoption and of parental recognition for same-sex partners shapes family formation, and the cohabitation agreement's inheritance treatment as siblinghood leaves surviving partners outside the spousal regime.
localsOnly:
Residents can register a contrat de vie commune before a notary and deposit it at the public registry, gaining a recognised cohabitation status but not marriage, and are assessed for inheritance tax as siblings rather than as spouses. The same instrument is available to siblings and to parents and children.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: a resident cannot amend the gender marker on civil-status records. Employment, education, housing and service discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity has no general statutory prohibition, and the school-sensitisation measure that would have covered it was dropped in the 2012 replacement bill.

Hate-speech and hate-crime provisions do protect sexual orientation, with penalties running from 6 months to 10 years depending on the offence. Whether those provisions extend to gender identity is not stated in the sources. Public visibility is constrained: roughly 10 people are openly out, no Pride is organised, and there are no official community venues, with community life concentrated in a small number of gay-friendly establishments.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on whether SOGI discrimination is prohibited: Outright International records no ban, Queer In The World records prohibitions in certain contexts. The scope of any sector-specific protection is unresolved in this inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses transgender-specific violence, incidents involving trans visitors, or enforcement of the hate-crime provisions against gender-identity-motivated conduct. The absence of reported anti-trans incidents reflects an absence of reporting in these sources, not a documented finding of safety.

Bathroom and facility access, document-marker rules for entry, visa and border screening that could disclose gender history, and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not sourced here and remain unverified. The claim that entry occurs across the French land frontier under a border-free zone derives from the prior profile text and is not restated in the current inventory.
